title: Family: who we are to each other, and the work that keeps a home going

summary.text: Every family runs on hours of cooking, washing and caring each day, and most of that work is never paid. In this unit you name your relatives and find that English has one word, uncle, for four different relations. You count and time every job done in your home for one evening, and draw a pictograph of who did what. You learn what parents and guardians must give a child, how girls and women were kept out of school and other rights, and how that is changing. You also meet animal families, where a father, a group or even another kind of bird raises the young.
summary.art: A busy kitchen and living room in an Indian flat seen from above, with a grandmother cooking, a mother bathing a toddler, a father washing tumblers and a girl with a notebook and a wall clock writing down times.

intro.hook: Who in your home works the most? Before you answer, think about yesterday. Who cooked, washed the vessels, folded clothes, and put the baby to sleep?
intro.text: A family is a group of people who look after each other. Some families are big, with grandparents, aunts and cousins under one roof. Some are small, with one parent and one child. In every family, someone cooks, cleans, shops and cares for the youngest and the oldest. This work takes many hours, and in most homes nobody is paid for it. In this unit you find out exactly how many minutes of work your own home needs in one evening, and who does it. You will be surprised.
intro.art: A girl at a dining table looking at a wall clock, with a notebook in front of her, while behind her people in her family cook, sweep and fold clothes.

outcomes: I can name the people in my family, say how each one is related to me, and use the right relation word in my home language and in English.
I can explain that families come in many shapes, such as joint, nuclear, one-parent and adoptive families, and that care is what holds each of them together.
I can count and time the jobs done in my home, show the minutes in a table and a pictograph, and say what the numbers show.
I can explain why unpaid home work and care work are real work, and say who does most of this work in India.
I can list what parents and guardians must give a child, and what a child can do for the family.
I can give examples of how girls and women were kept out of school and other rights in India, and how people such as Savitribai Phule changed this.
I can describe how some animals raise their young, and who helps them.

terms.meaning: A group of people who care for each other and are joined by birth, marriage, adoption or by choosing to live as a family.
terms.example: Kavya lives with her Amma, her Appa, her Ajji and her little brother. They are her family. Her Mama in Bengaluru is family too, though he lives far away.
terms.art: A family of five in a flat in Mysuru sitting together on a mat, eating from steel plates.

terms.meaning: A person who belongs to your family, even if they live far away.
terms.example: Your mother's brother, your father's sister and your cousins are all relatives.
terms.art: A family tree on paper with small faces in circles, joined by lines.

terms.meaning: All the people in a family who were born at about the same time. Grandparents are one generation, parents the next, and children the next.
terms.example: Ajji, Appa and Kavya belong to three different generations.
terms.art: Three steps going down: a grandmother on the top step, a father on the middle step, a girl on the bottom step.

terms.meaning: Your relatives through your mother are on your mother's side. Your relatives through your father are on your father's side.
terms.example: In Tamil, Mama is your mother's brother and Chithappa is your father's younger brother. In English, both are called uncle.
terms.art: A tree with two big branches, one labelled Amma's side and one labelled Appa's side.

terms.meaning: A joint family is a big family where grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins live together. A nuclear family is parents, or one parent, living with their children.
terms.example: Farhan lives with his grandparents, his parents, his uncle, his aunt and two cousins. That is a joint family.
terms.art: Two houses side by side: a big one with many people at the windows, and a small flat with three people.

terms.meaning: A grown-up who takes the place of a parent and is responsible for a child.
terms.example: Meenakshi's grandmother is her guardian, because her parents work in another country.
terms.art: A grandmother walking a girl to school, holding her hand and her school bag.

terms.meaning: Work that nobody pays money for, such as cooking for your own family, washing your own clothes or looking after a sick grandparent.
terms.example: When a house help washes the vessels, she is paid. When Amma washes the same vessels, nobody pays her. Both are doing work.
terms.art: Two pictures side by side of hands washing the same steel vessels, one with a small pile of coins next to them and one without.

terms.meaning: Looking after people who need help: feeding a baby, bathing a toddler, giving medicine, helping with homework, sitting with someone who is ill.
terms.example: Lakshmi spends half an hour each evening helping her grandfather with his eye drops and his walk. That is care work.
terms.art: A girl holding her grandfather's arm as he walks slowly down a corridor in a flat.

terms.meaning: Treating someone unfairly because of who they are, for example because she is a girl.
terms.example: Sending a son to school but keeping a daughter at home to do housework is discrimination.
terms.art: A boy walking to school with a bag, while his sister watches from the doorway holding a broom.

terms.meaning: Rights that every person has in the same way, whoever they are. India's Constitution gives women and men equal rights.
terms.example: Every girl and every boy in India from 6 to 14 has the right to go to school for free.
terms.art: A girl and a boy walking side by side to school, each with a bag.

explanations.context: This card is about what makes a group of people a family.
explanations.definition: A family is a group of people who care for each other and are joined by birth, marriage, adoption or by choosing to live as a family.
explanations.description: Families come in many shapes. A joint family has grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins under one roof. A nuclear family is parents and their children. Some children live with one parent, some with grandparents, and some were adopted. Some families live apart, with a parent working in another city or country. What makes all of these families is the same: the people in them look after each other.
examples: Farhan in Hyderabad lives in a joint family of eight people.
Divya in Kochi lives with her mother only. They are a family of two.
Arjun was adopted as a baby. His parents are his parents, just as much as anyone's.
explanations.art: Four small pictures of different families: a big joint family, a mother and daughter, two grandparents with a grandson, and a couple with an adopted baby.

explanations.context: This card is about how the people in a family are connected, and the words we use for them.
explanations.definition: A relation is the way two people in a family are connected, such as 'my mother's brother'. A relation word is the name we call them, such as Mama.
explanations.description: Each person has two parents, four grandparents and eight great-grandparents. Your relatives come through your mother's side and your father's side. Many Indian languages have a separate word for each relation. In Tamil, Mama is your mother's brother, Chithappa is your father's younger brother and Periyappa is your father's elder brother. Hindi has Mama, Chacha and Tau. English calls all of them uncle. The words tell you exactly how a person is related. Children also get about half of their genes from their mother and half from their father. Genes are the instructions inside every cell of a body.
examples: Tamil: Paati and Thatha are grandmother and grandfather. Athai is your father's sister.
Kannada: Ajji is grandmother.
Hindi: Bua is your father's sister and Mausi is your mother's sister.
explanations.art: A family tree with Tamil and English names under each face: Amma, Appa, Mama, Athai, Paati, Thatha.

explanations.context: This card is about the cooking, cleaning and caring done at home, and why it counts as work.
explanations.definition: Unpaid work is work done for your own home or family that nobody pays for. Care work is looking after people who need help.
explanations.description: Cooking, washing, cleaning, shopping and caring take hours every day in every home. When a house help or a cook does this work, she is paid. When a family member does the same work, nobody pays. When India adds up the value of all the work done in the country, it leaves out unpaid home work. In 2019, India's Time Use Survey asked people how they spent each minute of a day. It found that women who did unpaid home work spent about 299 minutes a day on it. Men who did any spent about 97 minutes.
examples: Cooking three meals for a family of five can take more than three hours a day.
Sitting with a sick grandparent at night is care work.
A house help who sweeps and mops is doing paid work. The same sweeping by Amma is unpaid work.
explanations.art: A bar chart drawn on a kitchen wall: a tall bar for women's minutes of home work and a short bar for men's.

explanations.concept: What parents and guardians must give a child
explanations.context: This card is about what parents and guardians are responsible for.
explanations.definition: Parents and guardians are responsible for a child's food, home, health, safety, schooling and love.
explanations.description: A child cannot feed, clothe or protect themself for many years. So parents and guardians must give enough good food, a safe home and clothes. They take the child to a doctor and get them vaccinated. A vaccine teaches the body to fight a disease before the child catches it. They must send every child to school, daughters and sons alike. In India, the Right to Education Act of 2009 says every child from 6 to 14 can go to school for free. The law also says children under 14 must not be sent to work for money. Parents also give time: talking, listening and helping a child to decide things. Children help the family too, with jobs that suit their age.
examples: Getting polio drops and other vaccines on time.
Sending a daughter to school just as a son is sent.
Listening when a child says they are scared.
explanations.art: A mother holding a girl's hand at a vaccination counter, with a school bag on the girl's back.

explanations.concept: Girls and women, then and now
explanations.context: This card is about how girls and women have been treated in India, and what has changed.
explanations.definition: Discrimination against girls and women means treating them unfairly because they are female, for example by giving them less schooling, food, money or say.
explanations.description: For a long time, many Indian families sent sons to school and kept daughters at home to work. In 1848 in Pune, Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule opened a school for girls. People threw mud and stones at Savitribai on her way to school, and she carried a spare sari to change into. In 1950, India's Constitution gave women and men equal rights. Many things have changed, but not all. In the 2011 Census, about 82 in every 100 men could read and write, but only about 65 in every 100 women. Women still do most of the unpaid work at home.
examples: Savitribai Phule, who opened a girls' school in Pune in 1848 and wrote poems.
In Kerala, more than 90 in every 100 women could read and write in the 2011 Census.
A daughter now has the same right as a son to go to school, by law.
explanations.art: Savitribai Phule walking to school with a cloth bag, and a group of girls waiting for her at the door.

explanations.concept: How animal families raise their young
explanations.context: This card is about how other animals care for their young, and who helps them.
explanations.definition: Parental care is everything a parent or helper does to keep the young alive until they can live on their own.
explanations.description: Animals share this work in many ways. A cow feeds her calf with her milk. A pair of house crows build the nest together, and both feed the chicks. A male emperor penguin keeps the egg warm on his feet for about two months while the mother is at sea. A mother mugger crocodile guards her nest and carries her hatchlings to the water in her mouth. Jungle babblers live in groups, and older birds in the group help to feed the chicks. An Asian koel lays her eggs in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the koel chicks as their own. An olive ridley turtle lays her eggs on a beach and swims away. Her hatchlings live on their own from the start.
examples: House crows: both parents feed the chicks.
Seahorses: the father carries the eggs in a pouch until they hatch.
Elephants: a herd of related females, led by an older female, looks after the calves together.
explanations.art: A row of animal families: two crows feeding chicks in a nest, a penguin father with an egg on his feet, a mugger crocodile with babies in her mouth, and jungle babblers feeding a chick together.

explanations.concept: Why human children need so many helpers
explanations.context: This card is about why people take so long to grow up, and who helps raise them.
explanations.description: A calf walks within hours of being born. A human baby takes about a year to walk and many more years to look after themself. Scientists are still arguing about how human families managed this for most of history.
examples: Grandmothers, aunts, older brothers and sisters often feed and carry babies in Indian families.
In many homes, a neighbour or a house help also cares for a child.

perspectives.who: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy, an American scientist who studies animals and people, in her book Mothers and Others (2009)
perspectives.explanation: Human mothers have always had help from others, such as grandmothers, fathers and older children. Without these helpers, our long childhood would not have been possible.

perspectives.who: Kristen Hawkes and her team, who studied the Hadza people of Tanzania
perspectives.explanation: Grandmothers matter most. Hadza grandmothers dig food for their grandchildren, so mothers can have the next baby sooner. This is called the grandmother idea.

perspectives.who: John Bowlby, a British doctor, in his early writing
perspectives.explanation: A baby needs one main carer, usually the mother, above all others. Later studies found that most babies attach to several people.

explanations.art: A baby being passed from a mother to a grandmother while an older sister holds out a toy.

agreed.text: Babies and children need comfort and touch from people who care for them, not only food.
agreed.evidence: Harry Harlow's studies of baby monkeys in the 1950s, John Bowlby's work, and Mary Ainsworth's studies of mothers and babies in Uganda and the United States.

agreed.text: In India, women do much more unpaid home work and care work than men.
agreed.evidence: India's Time Use Survey of 2019 found that women who did this work spent about 299 minutes a day on it, and men who did any spent about 97 minutes.

agreed.text: Each child gets about half of their genes from their mother and half from their father.
agreed.evidence: Studies of how features are passed on in families, and the reading of human DNA.

challenging.claim: Housework is not real work, because nobody is paid for it.
challenging.who: A common view, and the way countries add up their income
challenging.context: This card is about whether home work counts as work.
challenging.for: Nobody pays money for it, so it does not appear in a country's income figures.
challenging.against: The same jobs are paid when a house help or a cook does them. Without this work, nobody could eat, stay clean or go out to a paid job. Many countries now measure it with time use surveys.

challenging.claim: Hugging and comforting a child too much spoils them.
challenging.who: John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner Watson, in their book for parents, 1928
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of how to bring up children.
challenging.for: They thought children who were cuddled would grow up weak and clingy.
challenging.against: Harlow's baby monkeys ran to a soft cloth mother when scared. Children's studies since then show that comfort makes children braver, not weaker.

challenging.claim: A child needs only their mother to grow up well.
challenging.who: John Bowlby's early writing, in the 1950s
challenging.context: This card is about who a child needs.
challenging.for: Babies often cling most to one person, and are upset when that person goes away.
challenging.against: Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson followed babies in Glasgow in 1964 and found most of them grew attached to several people. Grandmothers, fathers and others raise children well.

big_questions.q: When a house help cooks, she is paid. When Ajji cooks the same meal, she is not. Is it the same work?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the food does for the family, and why one person gets money.

big_questions.q: Is a family made by birth, or by people caring for each other?
big_questions.hint: Think about an adopted child, or a grandmother who raises her granddaughter.

big_questions.q: Why does a human child need looking after for so many more years than a calf?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a child must learn before they can live on their own.

big_questions.q: A koel chick is raised by crows. Who is the koel's family?
big_questions.hint: Think about who fed the chick, and who laid the egg.

big_questions.q: If nobody counts a piece of work, is it still there?
big_questions.hint: Think about your own work count, and what would happen if a job was not done for a week.

story.title: Ajji's Minutes
story.note: The story is made up. What it shows is true: home work takes many hours, it is often unpaid, and many girls of earlier generations left school to do it.
text: Kavya was eight, and she lived in a flat in Mysuru with her Amma, her Appa, her Ajji and her little brother Chintu, who was three.
Amma was a nurse. That week she worked at night. Appa worked in a bank. Ajji was Appa's mother, and she had lived with them since Kavya was born.
One Saturday Kavya had a science job. She had to write down every home job done that day, who did it, and how many minutes it took.
She took a notebook and sat where she could see the kitchen clock.
Ajji was already awake. At half past five she swept the doorstep and drew a rangoli with white powder. Then she boiled the milk and made coffee for everyone. Kavya wrote it all down.
Gowramma came at seven to sweep and mop the floors. She worked for an hour, and Appa paid her at the end of every month. Kavya wrote, "Gowramma, 60 minutes, paid."
Amma came home from the hospital at eight. She was tired, but she bathed Chintu and fed him idli before she went to sleep. Kavya wrote, "Amma, 40 minutes."
Appa read the newspaper. Then he washed his own tiffin box. Kavya wrote, "Appa, 5 minutes."

All day the list grew. Ajji ground the batter, cut vegetables, cooked lunch, washed the vessels, folded the clothes and took Chintu to the park. When Chintu cried, Ajji picked him up. When the gas cylinder ran out, Ajji called the gas agency.
At night Kavya added up the minutes. She added them again, because she could not believe it.
"Ajji did six hours and ten minutes," she said. "Appa did thirty-five minutes. I did twenty."
Appa put down his phone. "Six hours?"
"And Gowramma did one hour, and she was paid," said Kavya. "Ajji, who pays you?"
Ajji laughed. "Nobody pays me, kanda. Nobody ever has."
"But it's the same work," said Kavya. "Gowramma sweeps, and you sweep."

Ajji sat down on the mat next to her. "When I was your age, I lived in a village near Mandya," she said. "I went to school until Class 4. Then my mother had my fourth brother, and she needed help at home. So I stayed home and looked after the babies. My brothers went to school."
"Did you want to go?" asked Kavya.
"I loved sums," said Ajji. "I was the fastest in my class. I still add the vegetable bill before the shopkeeper does."
"That's not fair," said Kavya.
"No," said Ajji. "It was not fair. Things are better now. Your Amma studied nursing. You will study whatever you like."

Kavya looked at her notebook. Every line was a job that had to be done, or nobody would have eaten, and nobody would have had clean clothes. Ajji's minutes had held up the whole day, and nobody had counted them before.
"Can I draw a picture of the minutes?" she asked. "One clock for every half hour?"
She drew it. Ajji's row had twelve clocks and a bit. Appa's row had one clock and a bit.
Appa looked at the picture for a long time. "I don't know how to make ragi mudde," he said at last.
"I will teach you," said Ajji. "Tomorrow."

The next evening Ajji stood next to Appa at the stove. She showed him how to stir the ragi flour into the boiling water with a wooden stick, fast, so no lumps formed. His first mudde was lumpy. His second was better. Chintu ate both.
Kavya stuck the picture on the fridge. A week later she did the count again. Appa's row had four clocks. Kavya's had two. Ajji's had nine.
That evening Ajji had an hour with nothing to do. She sat with Kavya at the table, and they did sums together. Ajji won.
story.epiphany: Work is work even when nobody pays for it. Ajji's minutes kept the whole family going, and they only became visible when Kavya counted them.
ask: Why did Kavya add up the minutes twice?
Why did Ajji leave school when she was a girl? Was that fair to her?
What changed in the family after Kavya drew the picture of the minutes?
Who taught Appa to make ragi mudde, and why do you think he had never learned?

games.title: Who Raises the Babies? An animal family matching game
games.context: This is a card game about animal families. You match each animal to the ones who look after their young.

printables.title: 12 animal cards to cut out (who looks after the young is on the back)

items.b: The mother. She feeds the calf with her milk.
Both parents. They build the nest together and both feed the chicks.
The father keeps the egg warm on his feet for about two months. Then both parents feed the chick.
The father. He carries the eggs in a pouch until they hatch.
The mother. She guards the nest and carries the hatchlings to water in her mouth.
A group. The parents and older birds in their group all feed the chicks.
House crows. The koel mother lays her egg in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the chick.
Nobody. The mother lays her eggs on a beach and swims away. The hatchlings live on their own.
A group. The calf's mother and the other related females in the herd look after the calf.
Both parents. The mother seals herself into a tree hole with the eggs. The father brings food to both.
Both parents. They take turns to bring insects to the chicks.
Parents and many helpers: grandparents, older children, relatives and others.

rules: Lay the 5 carer cards face up in a row.
Shuffle the 12 animal cards and put them in a pile, animal side up.
On your turn, take the top animal card. Place the card below the carer you think is right, and say why.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it under the right carer card.
The player with the most cards at the end wins. Playing with one grown-up, try to beat your own score in a second round.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay out the 5 carer cards. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: In this game you guess who looks after each animal's babies. Some answers will surprise you.
flow.kid: Who looks after each animal's babies? Guess, then turn the card over.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Raises the Babies, a matching game about animal families.

flow.do: Play the game. Each player places a card, says why, and then turns the card over.
flow.say: Before you turn it over, tell us why you chose that carer.
flow.kid: Pick a carer card. Say why. Then turn it over.
flow.parent: Many children put every animal under 'Mother'. The penguin, seahorse, babbler and koel cards show that this is not always so.

check.q: Who carries a seahorse's eggs until they hatch?
check.why: In seahorses, the father has a pouch, and he carries the eggs in it until they hatch. If you chose the mother, that is the usual guess, because in most animals she does it.

flow.do: Talk about the surprises.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? Under which card would you put our family?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? Where does our family go?

ask.q: Where would you put our family, and why?
good: Both parents, because Amma and Appa both look after us.
A group, because Paati and my aunt also look after me.

flow.think: The crows raised a koel chick. Did they know the chick was not theirs?

experiments.title: The Home Work Count: who keeps our home running in one evening?
experiments.context: In this experiment you write down every home job done in your home in one evening, who did it and how long it took.
experiments.question: How many minutes of home work does our home need in one evening, and who does it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Who will do the most minutes of home work this evening? How many minutes will all the jobs add up to? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Count every person in the same way: the job, the start time and the end time, all from the same clock. Count everyone, including yourself, any house help or cook, and anyone looking after a baby or an elder. Ask everyone to have a normal evening, so the count shows a usual day. Count from 5 o'clock until bedtime.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a wall clock, or a phone clock that the child can see
a sheet of paper and coloured pencils for the pictograph

experiments.safety: Nothing in this experiment is unsafe. The child watches jobs and writes. They do not need to go near the stove.

schedule.what: Guess first. Then write down every home job from 5 o'clock until bedtime. Add up the minutes for each person and draw a pictograph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a pictograph with one clock for every 15 minutes of work, one row for each person.

flow.do: 1. Sit together before 5 o'clock. 2. Ask your child to name the home jobs that happen in an evening. 3. Write their guesses in the notebook.
flow.say: Tonight we will count every home job and time it. First, guess. Who will do the most minutes of work? How many minutes will it be in all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tonight you count every home job. Guess first. Who will work the most? How many minutes in all? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that person will do the most?
good: Because Ajji does the cooking, and cooking takes long.
Because Amma comes home and starts the dinner and the washing.

flow.parent: Write down the guess with the reason. It is the child's prediction, and it matters more when it turns out wrong.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Home Work Count. You guess who will do the most home work this evening.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table in the notebook. 2. Tell the family about the count. 3. Ask everyone to have a normal evening.
flow.say: Please do everything as you always do. Kavya is only counting, not checking anyone.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Ask everyone to do what they always do.
flow.parent: This count is not about blaming anyone. Nobody should be told off for doing few minutes. If people change what they do because they are being watched, the count will not show a usual evening. Remember to count jobs such as feeding a baby, helping with homework and giving medicine. These are care work.

flow.do: 1. From 5 o'clock, each time someone starts a home job, your child writes the job, the person and the start time. 2. When the job ends, they write the end time. 3. Write whether the person is paid for it.
flow.say: Someone is starting the cooking. What time is it now? Write it down. Tell me when they finish.
flow.kid: Someone starts a job. Look at the clock. Write the time. Write it again when they stop.
flow.parent: Spread this over the evening. If reading the clock is hard, you can read out the times and your child writes the job and the person. If two jobs happen at once, write both. Count your child's own jobs too, such as setting the plates.

check.q: Ajji starts cooking at 6:10 and stops at 7:00. How long did she cook?
check.why: Count on from 6:10. To 6:30 is 20 minutes, and 6:30 to 7:00 is 30 more. 20 and 30 make 50 minutes. If you chose 10 minutes, you only looked at the minute numbers.

flow.do: 1. After the evening, work out the minutes for each job. 2. Add up the minutes for each person. 3. Write each person's total in a list.
flow.say: Now add up each person's minutes. Who did the most? Who did the least? Was any of it paid?
flow.kid: Add up each person's minutes. Who did the most?
flow.parent: Help with the adding if the numbers are big. In most Indian homes, one or two people, very often women, do most of the minutes. Your result may be different. Whatever you found is a real result.

flow.do: 1. Draw a pictograph. 2. Draw one clock for every 15 minutes, in one row for each person. 3. Draw part of a clock for a part of 15 minutes.
flow.say: Let's draw the minutes as clocks. One clock is 15 minutes. How many clocks does each person get?
flow.kid: Draw one clock for every 15 minutes. One row for each person.
flow.parent: If one person's total is 140 minutes, that is 9 clocks and a bit more, because 9 times 15 is 135.

flow.do: Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and a reason. Compare with the guess from the start.
flow.say: Was your guess right? What did the count show? Who was paid, and who was not? Why do you think it is like that?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Who did most? Who was paid?

ask.q: What did the count show you that you did not know before?
good: Ajji did much more work than I thought.
The jobs added up to more than three hours.
The house help is paid, but Amma is not, for the same kind of work.

flow.think: If nobody did any of these jobs for a week, what would our home be like?

experiments.title: Many Hands: do two people fold clothes twice as fast?
experiments.context: In this experiment you time how long it takes to fold a pile of clothes alone, with two people and with three.
experiments.question: If two people fold a pile of clothes together, do they finish in half the time?
experiments.predict: Guess how long it will take you to fold 20 clothes alone. Then guess how long it will take with two people, and with three. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same 20 clothes each time, and shake them out flat before each try. Fold them the same way each time. Time each try with the same clock. Fold alone at the start and again at the end, because practice can make you faster.

materials.item: 20 dry clothes from the washing, or 20 hand towels and handkerchiefs
a phone stopwatch or a wall clock with a second hand
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Nothing in this experiment is unsafe.

schedule.what: Fold the same 20 clothes alone, with two people, with three people, and alone again. Time each try.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, and draw a bar for each try.

flow.do: 1. Put 20 dry clothes in a heap on a mat or a bed. 2. Agree on one way to fold each kind. 3. Ask for guesses.
flow.say: How long will 20 clothes take you alone? With two people? With three? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How long will 20 clothes take you alone? With two? Why?
flow.parent: Write down the guesses. Most children guess that two people take exactly half the time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Many Hands test. You time how long it takes to fold clothes alone and with helpers.

flow.do: 1. Start the stopwatch. 2. Your child folds all 20 alone. 3. Stop it and write the time.
flow.say: Go! Fold as you always do, not in a rush.
flow.kid: Fold all 20 alone. Write the time.
flow.parent: If your child is very slow, use 10 clothes for every try instead. Keep the number the same for every try.

flow.do: 1. Shake out all the clothes. 2. Two people fold them together. Time it. 3. Shake them out again. 4. Three people fold them. Time it.
flow.say: Now we shake them out and fold together. Let's see if two of us take half the time.
flow.kid: Now fold with two people. Then with three. Time each one.

check.q: Alone, Divya took 8 minutes to fold the clothes. With her mother, they took 5 minutes. Was that exactly half the time?
options: No, half of 8 is 4, so it took a little longer than half
No, it took twice as long
check.why: Half of 8 minutes is 4 minutes. They took 5, which is more than half. Helpers can get in each other's way or wait for each other. If you chose 'Yes', check by doubling 5: that is 10, not 8.

flow.do: Shake out the clothes again. Your child folds all 20 alone a second time. Time it.
flow.say: One more alone. Were you faster this time? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Fold alone once more. Were you faster?
flow.parent: If the second try alone is much faster, practice helped. Compare the helper tries with the average of the two alone tries.

flow.do: Look at the results together. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: Did two people take exactly half the time? Did three take a third? Why not?
flow.kid: Did two of you take half the time? Why or why not?

ask.q: Why might two people not take exactly half the time?
good: Because we bumped into each other.
Because one of us was faster than the other.
Because we had to decide who folds what.

flow.think: Is the work of a home done faster when it is shared? Is it done more fairly?

activities.title: One Word, Four Uncles: the relation words in your home language
activities.context: In this activity you list your relatives and find the word for each one, in your home language and in English.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.

schedule.what: Make a table of relatives, with the relation, the word in your home language and the word in English.

activities.record: A table with three columns: how the person is related to me, our word, the English word.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with three columns: 'How they are related to me', 'Our word', 'English word'. 2. Fill in Amma's brother, Amma's sister, Appa's brother and Appa's sister.
flow.say: What do we call Amma's brother? And Appa's younger brother? Let's write our words, then the English words.
flow.kid: Write what you call Amma's brother. Then Appa's brother. Then the English words.
flow.parent: In Tamil, for example: Amma's brother is Mama, Appa's younger brother is Chithappa, Appa's elder brother is Periyappa, Appa's sister is Athai. In Hindi: Mama, Chacha, Tau, Bua. Use your own family's words.
flow.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You find the words your family uses for relatives.

flow.do: Add more rows: grandmothers and grandfathers on both sides, cousins, and the wives and husbands of aunts and uncles.
flow.say: What do you call Amma's mother? Appa's mother? Are they the same word?
flow.kid: Add your grandmothers. Is there one word or two?
flow.parent: In some languages there are two different words for the two grandmothers. In Telugu, for example, Ammamma is your mother's mother and Nannamma is your father's mother. English says grandmother for both.

flow.do: Count the people English calls uncle. Then count the words your language has for the same people.
flow.say: How many different people did English call uncle? How many words did our language use?
flow.kid: Count. How many people are 'uncle' in English? How many words do we have?

check.q: Arjun's Mama is his mother's brother. His Chithappa is his father's younger brother. What does English call both of them?
check.why: English uses one word, uncle, for a mother's brother, a father's brother and the husbands of aunts. Many Indian languages have a separate word for each, so the word tells you exactly how the person is related.

flow.think: Why might a language have so many words for relatives?

activities.title: Our Family Tree: three generations
activities.context: In this activity you draw your family tree, from your grandparents down to you.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper or newspaper
pencils and coloured pencils

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe. Ask before cutting any photo.

schedule.what: Draw a family tree with your grandparents at the top, your parents, aunts and uncles in the middle, and you and your cousins at the bottom.

activities.record: The family tree, with each person's name and their relation word.

flow.do: 1. At the top, draw both pairs of grandparents. 2. Below, draw the parents and their brothers and sisters. 3. At the bottom, draw your child, their brothers and sisters, and their cousins.
flow.say: Who is at the top of our tree? Who comes from Ajji and Thatha? Let's draw them in a row.
flow.kid: Draw your grandparents at the top. Then your parents. Then you.
flow.parent: Join people with lines: a line across for a married couple and a line down to their children. If your family has a different shape, such as one parent, adoption or step-parents, draw it the way it really is. Every shape is a real family tree.
flow.context: This is the first step of drawing your family tree, from grandparents to you.

flow.do: 1. Write each person's name and the word your child calls them. 2. Colour your mother's side one colour and your father's side another.
flow.say: Write what you call each person. Use one colour for Amma's side and another for Appa's side.
flow.kid: Write what you call each person. Colour Amma's side and Appa's side.

flow.kid: Two parents. Four grandparents. How many great-grandparents?

check.why: Each of your 4 grandparents had 2 parents, and 4 times 2 is 8. The number doubles every generation you go back. If you chose 6, you added 2 instead of doubling.

flow.think: If the number doubles each generation, how many people were your family 10 generations ago?

flow.say: Ask Paati what work she did at home when she was your age.
flow.kid: Ask: What work did you do at home at my age?

sketch pens

Turn the wheel and check yesterday's jobs were done.

challenges.title: A Dinner Everyone Helps Make
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You plan a simple dinner that every person in the family helps to make.
challenges.problem: In many homes one person makes the whole dinner. Plan a simple dinner that the whole family makes together in 30 minutes, with a safe job for every person, from the youngest to the oldest.
constraints: Every person has at least one job.
Only grown-ups use the stove, knives and the pressure cooker.
The dinner is ready in 30 minutes.
materials: the food your family usually eats
general: Make a list of jobs: washing, cutting, cooking, setting plates, serving, washing up.
Give each job to someone who can do it safely.
Put the jobs in order, so nobody waits too long.
creative: Give the youngest child a job that matters, such as tearing curry leaves or counting out the plates.
Choose a meal where most of the work is mixing, not cooking, such as curd rice with cucumber.
Make a picture menu so a child who cannot read yet knows their job.

flow.kid: Give each person a job. Is it safe for them?

flow.do: Make the dinner together, or plan it for tomorrow. Time how long it takes.
flow.say: Let's try it. Did it take less than 30 minutes?
flow.kid: Make it together. Time it.
flow.think: How did it feel to eat a meal everyone made?

quiz.p: Kavya counts the home work in her flat one evening. Her Ajji cooks for 70 minutes and nobody pays her. Their house help sweeps for 60 minutes and is paid. Who did work?
opts: Only the house help, because she was paid
Only Ajji, because she worked longer
quiz.why: Both did work. Cooking and sweeping both need time and effort, and the family needs both. Being paid or not does not change whether it is work. Choosing 'only the house help' means thinking only paid jobs count.

quiz.p: Farhan lives with his grandparents, his parents, his uncle, his aunt and two cousins in one home. What kind of family is this?
opts: Not a family, because there are too many people
quiz.why: A joint family has grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins under one roof. A nuclear family is only parents and their children.

quiz.p: Divya lives in Kochi with only her mother. Are they a family?
opts: Yes, because they live together and care for each other
No, a family needs a mother and a father
Only if grandparents live with them
quiz.why: Care is what makes a family, not how many people there are. A mother and a daughter are a family of two. Choosing 'No' means thinking there is only one shape of family.

quiz.p: In Tamil, Arjun calls his mother's brother Mama. What does English call this person?
quiz.why: English uses uncle for a mother's brother, a father's brother and the husband of an aunt. Tamil has a separate word for each.

quiz.p: Each person has 2 parents and 4 grandparents. How many great-grandparents does each person have?
quiz.why: Each of the 4 grandparents had 2 parents. 4 times 2 is 8. The number doubles each generation back. Choosing 6 means adding 2 instead of doubling.

quiz.p: India's Time Use Survey in 2019 found that women who did unpaid home work spent about 299 minutes a day on it. What did it find for men who did any?
quiz.why: Men who did any unpaid home work spent about 97 minutes a day. That is about one third of the women's 299 minutes. Women in India do most of this work.

quiz.p: Which of these must parents or guardians in India do for a child of 8?
opts: Send the child out to work for money
Keep the child at home to do housework
quiz.why: The Right to Education Act of 2009 says every child from 6 to 14 has the right to free schooling. Parents must send daughters and sons alike. Sending a child under 14 to work for money is against the law.

quiz.p: In 1848 in Pune, Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule did something new. What was it?
opts: They opened a school for girls
quiz.why: They opened a school for girls, at a time when most girls were not sent to school. People threw mud at Savitribai on her way to teach, but she kept going.

quiz.p: Harry Harlow gave baby monkeys two model mothers. One was wire and gave milk. One was soft cloth and gave no milk. Which did the babies cling to?
opts: The wire one, because it gave milk
quiz.why: The babies drank from the wire mother, then went back to cling to the cloth one, and ran to her when scared. Comfort mattered to them as much as food. Choosing the wire one is the old idea that babies love whoever feeds them.

quiz.p: An Asian koel lays her egg in a house crow's nest. Who feeds the koel chick?
quiz.why: The crows raise the koel chick along with their own chicks. The koel mother does not come back to feed the chick.

quiz.p: Who keeps an emperor penguin egg warm through the cold winter?
opts: The egg is left on the ice alone
quiz.why: The father holds the egg on his feet under a fold of skin for about two months. The mother is at sea, feeding. Choosing 'the mother' is the usual guess, because in many animals she does it.

quiz.p: Meena and her brother fold 20 clothes together. Alone, Meena took 10 minutes. What is the most likely time for the two of them?
quiz.why: Two people often take a little more than half the time, because they wait for each other or get in each other's way. Exactly 5 minutes would happen only if both worked at the same speed with no waiting.

worksheets.title: Who Does the Work at Home? (core)

items.p: Lakshmi times her Amma washing the vessels. Amma starts at 8:15 and finishes at 8:40. How long did Amma wash the vessels?
items.why: Count on from 8:15: to 8:30 is 15 minutes, and to 8:40 is 10 more. 15 and 10 make 25. A strong answer counts on from the start time.

items.p: Cooking for your own family is work, even when nobody pays for it.
items.why: True. It takes time and effort, and the family cannot eat without it. Paid or unpaid, it is work.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: people in a family born at about the same time
a grown-up who takes the place of a parent
looking after people who need help
someone who belongs to your family
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit.

items.p: A family with grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins under one roof is called a ____ family.
items.why: A joint family has several generations and branches living together.

items.p: Sort these jobs. Is each one paid or unpaid?
items: a house help sweeping the floor for a salary
Ajji cooking lunch for the family
a cook making dinner in someone else's home
a nurse giving medicine in a hospital
items.a: see items
items.why: The same kind of job can be paid or unpaid. It is paid when someone outside the family is given money to do it. A strong sorter looks at who pays, not at the job.

items.p: In your Home Work Count, who did the most minutes of work? Write the number of minutes, and one reason why that person did the most.
items.a: For example: Ajji did 150 minutes, because she cooks dinner and puts Chintu to sleep.
items.why: A strong answer gives the real number from the count and a reason that comes from what the child saw.

items.p: Draw your family tree with three generations: grandparents at the top, parents in the middle, and you at the bottom. Write what you call each person.
items.a: A tree with grandparents at the top, parents in the middle and the child at the bottom, with relation words.
items.why: A strong tree joins couples with a line across and children with a line down, and shows both sides of the family.

items.p: In Hindi, Bua is your father's sister and Mausi is your mother's sister. What does English call both of them?
items.why: English uses aunt for both. Hindi has two words, so the word tells you which side of the family she is on.

items.p: A baby monkey in Harlow's study loved the wire mother most, because she gave milk.
items.why: False. The babies drank from the wire mother but clung to the soft cloth mother, and ran to her when scared.

items.p: Treating someone unfairly because of who they are, for example because she is a girl, is called ____.
items.why: Discrimination means unfair treatment because of who a person is.

items.p: Three of these are jobs a parent or guardian must do for a young child. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Send the child to work in a shop
items.why: Vaccines, school and good food are what a child needs. Sending a child under 14 to work for money is against the law in India.

items.p: Here is a picture of a family tree with three rows. Label each row with its generation: grandparents, parents or children.
items.why: Each row of a family tree is one generation. The oldest are at the top.
items.art: A simple family tree with three rows of faces joined by lines, with an empty label box beside each row.

items.p: Kavya's Ajji left school after Class 4 to look after her baby brothers, while her brothers went to school. Was that fair? Give a reason.
items.a: No. Ajji wanted to learn and loved sums, but she lost her schooling only because she was a girl.
items.why: A strong answer says it was unfair and gives the reason: the choice was made because she was a girl, not because of what she wanted or could do.

items.p: Meenakshi and her brother Arjun disagree about who should wash the dinner plates.

views.says: Amma cooked dinner, so the rest of us should wash up. That way everyone does a share.
Amma is the fastest at washing up, so it makes sense for her to do it. We would be slow and break things.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from your Home Work Count. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, for example that Amma already did the most minutes in the count. It also says what the other side has right: Arjun is right that some jobs go faster with practice, and Meenakshi is right that sharing makes it fairer.
items.why: Both have a point. Being fastest is a reason, but it can also mean one person ends up doing everything. Practice makes other people faster too.

items.p: Put the steps of the Home Work Count in order.
items: Guess who will do the most
Write the start and end time of each job
Draw a pictograph of the minutes
a: Guess who will do the most
Write the start and end time of each job
Draw a pictograph of the minutes
items.why: You guess first, so the guess is a real prediction. Then you collect the times, add them up, and show them.

items.p: Gowramma sweeps Kavya's flat and is paid. Ajji sweeps the same floor on Sundays and is not paid. Write why both are doing work.
items.a: Both use time and effort, and the floor gets clean either way. Whether someone pays does not change what the work does for the family.
items.why: A strong answer says the work is the same job with the same result, and only the payment is different.

items.p: When India adds up the value of all the work done in the country in a year, which of these is left out?
opts: A cook paid to make meals in a hotel
Ajji cooking lunch for her own family
items.why: Unpaid home work is left out. So cooking, cleaning and caring for your own family are not counted, though every family needs them. The paid cook and the factory are counted.

items.p: In a Home Work Count, Amma did 90 minutes, Appa did 30 minutes, Paati did 120 minutes and the child did 15 minutes. How many minutes of home work were done in all?
items.why: 90 + 30 + 120 + 15 = 255 minutes. That is 4 hours and 15 minutes in one evening. A strong answer also says who did the most.

items.p: In the Many Hands test, three people took longer than a third of the time one person took. Give two reasons why.
items.a: They had to wait for each other, they got in each other's way, and some folders were slower than others.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons that come from what really happens when people work together.

items.p: Two grown-ups in a family talk about how to share the home work.

views.who: Shalini, who works in an office
views.says: We should share every job equally, half each, so that it is fair.

views.who: Rekha, her sister-in-law, who stays home with the children
views.says: It is fair if each person does what they are best at. I cook well, so I cook, and she earns money for the family.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that splitting by skill can leave one person with far more hours. It also says what the other side has right: Rekha is right that skills differ, and Shalini is right that hours should be fair.
items.why: This is a real disagreement among economists and families. A fair answer looks at hours as well as skills.

items.p: An olive ridley turtle mother stays with her hatchlings until they can swim.
items.why: False. She lays her eggs on a beach and swims away. The hatchlings find their way to the sea on their own.

items.p: Match each animal to who looks after their young.
pairs: the parents and older birds in the group
the mother feeds the calf her milk
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Animals share the care of their young in very different ways.

items.p: John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner Watson wrote a book for parents in 1928. What did they tell parents?
opts: Do not hug or kiss your children
items.why: They told parents not to hug or kiss their children. Later studies, such as Harlow's, showed that comfort and touch are what children need.

items.p: Draw a pictograph of these minutes, with one clock for every 15 minutes: Ajji 60 minutes, Appa 30 minutes, Kavya 15 minutes.
items.a: Ajji: 4 clocks. Appa: 2 clocks. Kavya: 1 clock.
items.why: 60 divided by 15 is 4, 30 divided by 15 is 2, and 15 divided by 15 is 1. A strong pictograph has a key that says one clock is 15 minutes.

items.p: Each child gets about half of their genes from their mother and about half from their ____.
items.why: Genes come from both parents, about half from each.

items.p: Kerala had more women who could read and write than any other state in the 2011 Census. What could have helped girls there go to school?
items.a: For example: many schools close to home, families who wanted their daughters to study, and women who were teachers.
items.why: A strong answer gives reasons a child can think through, such as schools nearby and families choosing to send girls. Scientists still study exactly why.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a right every child in India has by law, or a job a child can help with at home?
cats: A job a child can help with
items: A job a child can help with
not being sent to work under 14
A job a child can help with
A job a child can help with
items.a: see items
items.why: A child has rights that grown-ups must protect, and can also help the family with jobs that suit their age.

items.p: Three of these are care work. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Feeding, giving medicine and helping with homework are all looking after someone who needs help. Watching cricket is rest, which everyone also needs.

items.p: Here is a picture of a family tree. Label the two sides of the family.
labels: The left branch, with Amma's parents
The right branch, with Appa's parents
items.why: Relatives through your mother are on your mother's side, and relatives through your father are on your father's side.
items.art: A family tree with two big branches, the left one with a grandmother and grandfather marked 'Amma's parents', the right one marked 'Appa's parents', and empty label boxes.

items.p: Which is the best reason to do the Home Work Count on a normal evening, not a festival day?
opts: So the count shows a usual day
Because clocks do not work on festivals
items.why: On festival days there is often much more cooking and cleaning. A normal evening shows what a usual day needs. That makes it a fair test.

items.p: Many people say a mother who stays at home 'does not work'. Use evidence from your Home Work Count to explain whether that is true.
items.a: It is not true. In our count, the person at home did many minutes of cooking, washing and caring. That is work. It is just unpaid.
items.why: A strong answer uses real numbers from the count and says the difference is payment, not work.

items.p: Three people talk about why human children need so many years of care.

views.who: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy, a scientist who studies animals and people
views.says: Human mothers always had help from grandmothers, fathers and older children. That help made our long childhood possible.

views.who: Kristen Hawkes, a scientist who studied Hadza grandmothers in Tanzania
views.says: Grandmothers matter most. They find food for grandchildren, so mothers can care for new babies.

views.who: John Bowlby, in his early writing
views.says: A baby needs one main carer above all, usually the mother.

items.ask: Whose idea fits your own family best? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one idea and links it to real people in the child's family, such as a grandmother who cooks. It also says what another view has right, for example that babies often do cling most to one person.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Each idea fits some families and some evidence.

items.p: The koel chick is raised by crows that did not lay the egg. An adopted child is raised by parents who did not give birth to them. What makes someone a parent?
items.a: For example: a parent is the one who feeds, protects and cares for a child every day, whoever gave birth.
items.why: A strong answer uses both examples and says what parents do, not only who gave birth. There is more than one good answer.

items.p: In the 2011 Census, about 82 in every 100 men in India could read and write, and about 65 in every 100 women. What is the best explanation?
opts: Women are not as good at learning to read
For many years, fewer girls were sent to school
Women did not want to read
items.why: For many years, many families kept daughters at home to work, so fewer women learned to read. It is about who got the chance, not about ability.

items.p: A family's Home Work Count showed 240 minutes in one evening. If the family does this every evening, how many minutes is that in a week?
items.why: 240 times 7 is 1680 minutes, which is 28 hours. A strong answer also says that this is more than a whole day and night of work each week, in one evening slot alone.

items.p: If every person in your home stopped all unpaid home work for one week, what would happen? Name three things.
items.a: For example: no cooked food, dirty plates and clothes piling up, a baby or grandparent not looked after, and nobody able to go out to a paid job.
items.why: A strong answer shows that paid work and school depend on unpaid home work being done.

items.p: Draw a bar chart of the Many Hands test: one person, two people and three people. Use your own times, or these: 10 minutes, 6 minutes, 5 minutes.
items.a: Three bars of 10, 6 and 5, getting shorter, but not halving each time.
items.why: A strong chart has labels on both axes and shows that adding helpers saves time, but less and less with each extra person.

items.p: Selvi folded 20 clothes alone in 12 minutes, then with her aunt in 7 minutes, then alone again in 9 minutes. Why was her second try alone faster than her first?
items.why: She had folded the same clothes twice before, so she had practised. This is why the test folds alone at the start and the end.

items.p: India's Constitution, from 1950, gives women and men equal rights.
items.why: True. The Constitution says nobody can be treated unfairly by the government because of their sex. But laws alone do not change every home.

items.p: Savitribai Phule kept teaching though people threw mud at her. Why do you think some people were so against girls going to school?
items.a: For example: they thought girls should only do housework, they were afraid of change, or they wanted girls to depend on others.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real reason people held then, and does not make it seem like the reason was right.

items.p: Here is a picture of the results table from the Home Work Count. Label the column that shows how you know who was paid.
items.why: The last column records whether the person is paid for the job. A strong answer also says that the 'Minutes' column comes from the start and end times.
items.art: A results table with six empty columns and an arrow pointing to one of them.

items.p: Match each person to what they found or did.
pairs: opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848
found baby monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother
showed babies use a trusted grown-up as a safe base
studied how Hadza grandmothers feed grandchildren
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these people changed how we understand families.

items.p: Sort these animals. Does the father help to look after the young, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: In penguins, crows and seahorses the father cares for the eggs or young. A bull does not look after the calf, and turtle hatchlings get no care at all.

items.p: A survey that asks people how they spent every part of their day is called a time ____ survey.
items.why: A time use survey shows how many minutes people spend on paid work, home work, care, rest and sleep.

items.p: A scientist wants to know if fathers in a city do more home work than fathers did 20 years ago. What is the best way to find out?
opts: Ask one father what he thinks
Compare time use surveys from 20 years ago and today
items.why: Time use surveys measure the minutes for many people in the same way, so you can compare them fairly across years. One person's opinion is not enough.

applications: Governments use time use surveys to plan for childcare, water taps near homes and cooking gas, which save women hours of unpaid work every day.
Doctors and hospitals now let parents stay with young children in hospital, because studies showed children suffer when kept apart from their carers.
Schemes that pay for girls' schooling and bicycles for girls going to school are based on studies of why girls drop out.
Family trees help doctors understand illnesses that run in families.
Adoption laws protect children who need a family, and make adoptive parents full parents.

open_questions.q: Why do human children take so many years to grow up, when most animals grow up in months?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, such as big brains that need time to learn, and grandmothers who help. Nobody knows which matters most.

open_questions.q: What is the fairest way to share home work in a family?
open_questions.why_open: Families, economists and thinkers disagree. Some say half each, some say by skill, and some say by how much time each person has.

open_questions.q: Do crows know that a koel chick in their nest is not theirs?
open_questions.why_open: Some birds throw out eggs that look different. House crows often raise koel chicks. How much they notice, and what they feel about it, is not known.

jokes.a: To remind him it was his turn to cook.

jokes.j: Why did Kavya bring a clock to dinner?
jokes.a: She wanted to count the minutes of everyone's work.

jokes.j: What did the broom say to the mop?

jokes.j: Why did the family tree go to school?
jokes.a: To learn more about its roots.

jokes.j: Why did the penguin father never get cold feet?
jokes.a: He had an egg to keep warm on them.

jokes.j: Why was the koel chick so big in the crow's nest?

Why did the seahorse father look so tired?

maths.problem: In Kavya's Home Work Count, Ajji did 135 minutes, Amma did 60 minutes, Appa did 30 minutes and Kavya did 15 minutes. In a pictograph, one clock is 15 minutes. How many clocks does each person get?
maths.explain: 135 divided by 15 is 9, because 9 times 15 is 135. 60 divided by 15 is 4. 30 divided by 15 is 2. 15 divided by 15 is 1.
maths.context: This is about the Home Work Count, where you time every home job in one evening.
maths.why_maths: A pictograph shows at a glance who did the most, without reading every number.

maths.problem: Ajji starts making dinner at 6:20 and finishes at 7:35. How long did she cook?
maths.answer: 1 hour and 15 minutes, which is 75 minutes.
maths.explain: From 6:20 to 7:20 is 1 hour. From 7:20 to 7:35 is 15 more minutes. 60 and 15 make 75 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the Home Work Count, where you write the start and end time of each job.
maths.why_maths: Counting on from a start time to an end time turns two clock readings into the minutes a job really took.

maths.problem: In the Many Hands test, Meena folded 20 clothes alone in 10 minutes. With her sister they took 6 minutes. With three people they took 5 minutes. How much time did the second helper save? How much did the third helper save?
maths.answer: The second helper saved 4 minutes. The third helper saved only 1 more minute.
maths.explain: 10 minus 6 is 4 minutes saved. 6 minus 5 is only 1 more minute. Each extra helper saved less time than the one before.
maths.context: This is about the Many Hands test, where you time folding clothes alone and with helpers.
maths.why_maths: Taking one time from another shows how much each helper really changed, which a list of times hides.

maths.problem: You have 2 parents, 4 grandparents and 8 great-grandparents. How many great-great-grandparents do you have? How many generations back do you go before you have more than 100 ancestors in one generation?
maths.answer: 16 great-great-grandparents. At 7 generations back you have 128, which is more than 100.
maths.explain: The number doubles each generation: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The seventh number, 128, is the first one over 100.
maths.context: This is about the family tree, where each person has two parents.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling pattern lets you work out your ancestors without drawing a giant tree.

roots.context: We have named our relatives, counted every minute of home work in one evening, and met animal families. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your count found that cooking, washing and caring take hours in a home every evening. A house help is paid for this work, but a family member doing it is not. When India adds up the value of all its work, it leaves out unpaid home work. So the work that keeps every family alive is missing from the count.
deep_truth.habit: We use the word 'work' for a paid job. People say 'Appa goes to work' and 'Amma doesn't work', even when Amma works for hours at home. The word hides the work that everything else depends on.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Home Work Count, the jobs added up to hours in one evening, and only a house help, if there was one, was paid. India's Time Use Survey of 2019 found women doing about 299 minutes of unpaid home work a day.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who has been fed, washed and carried by other people's hands, every day of your life.
three.what_is_life: Every young being, a crow chick, a calf or you, stays alive because someone gives them time and care.
three.what_is_this_world: It is a world where some of the most needed work is done without pay, and often without being counted.

roots.thread: A home looks like one thing from outside. Inside, it is many people and many jobs: one person cooks, one washes, one carries the baby, one earns money. Each job needs the others. A crow pair building a nest, a group of babblers feeding chicks and a family sharing dinner are the same care, done by many bodies. The one life of a family shows up as many hands.

teachings.teaching: Help given to you when you had done nothing for the helper is so great that even the earth and the sky together cannot repay it.
teachings.link: Most of the minutes in the Home Work Count are help of this kind. They are given every day, and the person who receives them, often a child, has done nothing to earn them.

teachings.teaching: A teacher tells students who are leaving: treat your mother as a god, treat your father as a god, treat your teacher as a god, treat your guest as a god.
teachings.link: The mother is named first. The work count shows one reason why: in many homes, her minutes are the ones the whole day stands on.

teachings.source: Ubuntu, a teaching of the Nguni-speaking peoples of southern Africa
teachings.teaching: A person is a person through other people.
teachings.link: Nobody grows up alone. Human children, like jungle babbler chicks, are raised by many helpers.

science.text: Countries leave unpaid home work and care out of their income figures. They measure it separately, with time use surveys.
Human mothers have always raised children with help from others, such as grandmothers, fathers and older children. Scientists still argue about which helpers mattered most.

other_view.who: Gary Becker, an American economist, in A Treatise on the Family (1981)
other_view.view: It can make sense for one person in a family to do most of the home work and another to earn money, because each gets good at their part. On this view, an unequal split of minutes is not always unfair, if the family chose it and shares what it earns.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat. The Home Work Count needs only a notebook and a clock the child can see. Counting from 5 o'clock to bedtime keeps it to one evening, and a grown-up can read out times if the child cannot yet read a clock. The parent note asks the family to act as usual and says the count is not about blame. Homes with a house help or cook count her too, which shows the same job paid and unpaid. The Many Hands test uses 20 clothes from the washing and folds alone at the start and the end, because practice speeds people up. Pallanguzhi can be played with 14 katoris or circles drawn on paper and tamarind seeds or rajma. The interview about schooling is marked for a grown-up, because answers can be painful. The spine is the intro, One Word Four Uncles, the Home Work Count, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1928, John B. Watson, a famous American psychologist, wrote a book for parents with Rosalie Rayner Watson. It told them never to hug or kiss their children. Many scientists then thought a baby loves their mother only because she feeds them. In the 1950s, Harry Harlow tested this idea at the University of Wisconsin in the United States. He took baby rhesus monkeys from their mothers and gave each baby two model mothers. One was made of wire and held a bottle of milk. The other was covered in soft cloth and gave no milk. The babies drank from the wire mother, then went straight back to cling to the cloth one. When something frightened them, they ran to the cloth mother. Harlow reported this in 1958, in a talk called The Nature of Love. Comfort mattered to the babies as much as food. John Bowlby in Britain, and Mary Ainsworth, who worked with him, showed that human children also need a trusted carer to feel safe. Harlow's experiments hurt the baby monkeys, and many scientists today say they were cruel.
how_we_found_out.who: John B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner Watson, Harry Harlow at the University of Wisconsin, John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought babies love their mother only because she feeds them, and that hugging spoils children. Harlow's baby monkeys chose a soft cloth mother with no milk over a wire mother with milk, and ran to her when afraid.
